records.themeTitle: The cry that remains in concealment
records.themeSummary: Concern for Heaven's honor can itself open a path of return when a person feels no connection.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef develops the same verse in Hosea by distinguishing consciously asking Hashem to fill one's lack from concealment so deep that no connection is felt. Even there, the cry that Heaven's honor remains incomplete is itself a way back. This explains the siman's insistence that the very place called ‘not My people’ becomes the place of renewed sonship.
records.targetEnglish: This was fixed here in the census of the wilderness generation. Through their service they illuminated that no unfolding in the world lies outside words of Torah. It was thereby established for all later generations that even in the greatest concealment, it cannot be that a person has no way to return to Hashem's light: a path back always remains, although he himself recognizes no connection. Nevertheless, Israel retains the cry, ‘What will You do for Your great name?’ On his own account he is ready to accept all the suffering; what he lacks is, ‘What will You do for Your great name?’ Since Hashem established in this world that Heaven's honor is, as it were, incomplete and Israel completes it through service, he therefore cries that Heaven's honor is incomplete. From this very cry he has a way to return to Hashem's light.

records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Lech Lecha 6
records.themeTitle: Rule over oneself before rule over others
records.themeSummary: The kingship verse makes self-government the first condition of authority.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach examines the word order in the same verse that opens this siman. A person must first govern his own desire before being entrusted with governing others. This gives a positive account of authority grounded in Torah alongside the siman's account of borrowed authority and words spoken without understanding.
records.targetEnglish: It is written (Proverbs 8:15), ‘By Me kings reign.’ In ordinary syntax it could have said, ‘By Me reign kings.’ This hints that the Holy One appoints as king only someone who can first rule over himself; him He appoints over others, as it says (Avot 4:1), ‘Who is mighty? One who conquers his inclination.’ ‘By Me kings reign’ means: someone who rules himself, whose understanding governs his desire, will then reign—he will be king over all. He need not heed the person opposing him, since his entire intention is for Heaven.

records.themeTitle: Derech eretz as sustaining an inhabited world
records.themeSummary: The term concerns constructive earthly life and has a limit distinct from indulgence.
records.explanation: Yisrael Kedoshim defines derech eretz through the settlement of the world, distinguishing necessary activity from immersion in surplus desire. It explains the barren-field image and why this conduct can prepare a person for Torah. The siman adds the decisive inward qualification: recognizing Hashem as the source of earthly life.
records.targetEnglish: Derech eretz is what is needed for the settlement of the land and the world, for ‘He did not create it for emptiness, but formed it to be inhabited’ (Isaiah 45:18). Through it a person's household is settled. This is the meaning of derech eretz everywhere: engaging in the world's settlement, as Berakhot 35b says, ‘Conduct them according to derech eretz,’ and Kiddushin 40b says, ‘Someone who is not involved in derech eretz is not part of the settled world.’ Immersion in desires unnecessary for the world's settlement is the opposite of derech eretz. Avraham our father therefore chose the land of Israel: he saw them weeding and working, unlike those eating, drinking and behaving frivolously, as Bereishit Rabbah 39:8 says. He saw that they had the derech eretz preceding Torah (Vayikra Rabbah 9:3), and understood that this was the land prepared for Torah, for ‘Without derech eretz there is no Torah’ (Avot 3:17).

records.themeTitle: Desire used according to Hashem's will
records.themeSummary: Surrender of desire means being willing to refrain and then receiving Torah's direction for the same power.
records.explanation: Divrei Soferim explains what it means to hand desire back to Hashem: even at its strongest, the person is willing to refrain when it conflicts with His will. Torah then directs the use of that power. This develops the siman's claim that desire ordered to Hashem's will can be united with awe rather than simply opposed to it.
records.targetEnglish: This is surrendering all desires to Hashem: even at the utmost force of desire, a person is ready to refrain if it is not according to Hashem's will. As the Midrash says (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 7; Midrash Tehillim 2) concerning ‘fenced with roses’: after incurring many expenses and approaching his wife, she says, ‘I saw [blood] red as a rose’; he turns aside. What thorn pricked him? Only words of Torah, soft as a rose. This is the meaning of Shavuot's two loaves being leavened: offering to Hashem the leaven in the dough that holds one back, as Berakhot 17a says. Through this one merits receiving Torah, the seasoning for the inclination (Kiddushin 30b)—using it only according to Hashem's will. Then it is ‘very good,’ as Bereishit Rabbah teaches; and as Berakhot 34a says of leaven, a little is beneficial, while much is harmful.

records.themeTitle: The awe that is itself called wisdom
records.themeSummary: Preparation of heart and received wisdom form a connected movement into action.
records.explanation: Divrei Soferim identifies the first wisdom as awe itself: preparing the heart not to act against Hashem's will. Received Torah then tells the person how to direct deeds and thoughts. This explains the siman's reciprocal relation of awe and wisdom without treating either as a dispensable addition to the other.
records.targetEnglish: A person's principal power is the desire and yearning within him and his preparing himself to receive and fulfill the whole Torah. The rest comes from Hashem, Who completes it for him and gives wisdom. But He ‘gives only to the wise’: those who possess the beginning of wisdom, awe of Hashem, which is itself also called wisdom, as it says, ‘Behold, awe of Hashem is wisdom.’ This is preparing the heart not to do anything against Hashem's will. Then all Torah and wisdom is entrusted to him, to know Hashem's will and to have all his deeds and thoughts conform to Hashem's wisdom within him.

records.targetRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 18:3
records.themeTitle: Possessions as an expansion of the person's point
records.themeSummary: The person's later acquisitions are described as connected to the life initially given to him.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov describes possessions as included in the person's original point of life and later gathered into its expansion. This explains why the siman distinguishes a desire for property from holiness reaching the property itself. Its final degree of love still remains, as the siman expressly says, a gift requiring help from Heaven.
records.targetEnglish: Even when a person is born, all the possessions and expansions are already included in him. But because his life is then constricted in the smallness of the point, the possessions stand at a distance. After the person grows, Hashem gives desire and yearning within that point to draw in, gather and bring close all the possessions belonging to the point and included in it. Then the person and all his possessions are joined together, and he is called ‘a new creature.’

records.themeTitle: The same love terms in a different classification
records.themeSummary: Great love and everlasting love can describe different distinctions according to the argument.
records.explanation: The terms need to be read in context. This siman distinguishes hidden love, revealed intensity and love's endurance through changing conditions. Sod Yesharim instead calls the revealed upper root great love and the clothed levels everlasting love or small love. Its measure is concealment and revelation. The shared names therefore do not justify treating the two classifications as an identical fixed hierarchy.

records.themeTitle: Connection together with awe
records.themeSummary: Joyful connection and reverent distinction must qualify each other.
records.explanation: Resisei Layla interprets Mishkan and Mikdash as connection and separation, two aspects that remain true together. It uses the same combination of joy and awe and warns against either isolated extreme. This develops the siman's distinction between an ideal order and the practical balancing required by a person's present deficiencies.
records.targetEnglish: Mikdash means a place of holiness: it is the opposite of Mishkan, for holiness means distinction and separation, while dwelling means being present and joined, without separation, as it says, ‘Who dwells with them amid their impurities’ (Yoma 56b). Holiness, by contrast, separates from impurity. Yet we find Mishkan called Mikdash and Mikdash called Mishkan (beginning of Eruvin): all is one, and both are true together. The Holy One dwells within Israel and is also distinct from them. As Tanna Devei Eliyahu Rabbah says (beginning of chapter 3), ‘I feared from within my joy and rejoiced from within my fear.’ Joy between companions proceeds from love and connection; awe proceeds from respect for someone greater and distinct. With Hashem both are together, and neither suffices without the other. Awe alone brings folly, as in ‘Is not your fear your folly?’ Joy alone brings levity. Of this the Sages said (Shabbat 31a), ‘Better that you had not brought it up,’ for Torah is called ‘rejoicing the heart,’ and through it one connects with Hashem.

records.themeTitle: The life hidden behind the dream image
records.themeSummary: Interpreting the surface rightly means recognizing the divine word that sustains it.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach extends the dream image to ordinary experience, using bread as its concrete example. Recognizing the divine word within it reveals a deeper life than the surface impression. This illustrates the siman's distinction between an image and the truth concealed within it. The siman's restrictions concerning who can discern such mixtures remain essential.
records.targetEnglish: ‘You hear a dream and interpret it.’ All the affairs of this world are like a dream needing interpretation, and as a person interprets it, so it is established for him. Someone who understands in everything that it is only from Hashem and that everything lives by what proceeds from His mouth understands the meaning in each thing and reaches true life. In bread, for example, what principally gives life is what proceeds from Hashem's mouth. Someone eating simply like an animal receives from bread only this world's life. Someone understanding that what proceeds from Hashem's mouth gives life attains enduring life. Bread, lechem, has the letters of dream, chalom: it needs interpretation. So too with all enjoyments, for all this world's pleasures and benefits are compared to bread.

records.themeTitle: Fulfilled truth and a deeper enduring truth
records.themeSummary: A dream can be fulfilled and still not express the deepest lasting level.
records.explanation: Machshavot Charutz preserves both sides of Yosef's dreams: they truly came about, yet the kingship they depicted was temporary. This provides a concrete comparison for the siman's claim that what counts as Torah thought at one level may still be called imagination from a deeper one. Calling it imagination does not mean every part of it was simply false.
records.targetEnglish: Nevertheless, it was still imagination, and the brothers' thought was not false either, for there truly are degrees. Although it was not an entirely false imagining, since it was fulfilled, it was still not complete truth that would endure forever, in the manner of ‘A truthful lip is established forever’ (Proverbs 12:19). Yosef's kingship lasted only for a time and in this world. The enduring kingship belongs to King David, from Yehudah's seed.

records.themeTitle: Imagining an unearned higher station
records.themeSummary: Pride lets the person picture himself beyond the level he can presently sustain.
records.explanation: Machshavot Charutz identifies the serpent's promise as the model for imagining oneself at a level that is not one's own. This explains the siman's relation between pride, illusion and receiving more light than the vessel can contain. The subsequent humility is therefore a correction of the person's claim and capacity, not merely a change in outward status.
records.targetEnglish: This is the imagining the serpent introduced by saying, ‘You shall be like God…’: it is the root of the empty thoughts, vanities and imaginings within a person—picturing himself at a level or condition above him, which is not fitting for him, each person according to his understanding.

records.themeTitle: The Giver awakens the cry for freedom
records.themeSummary: Recognizing the lack of freedom is itself the beginning of the rescue.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef develops the same cry in Egypt. Because Israel is free at the root, Hashem awakens the awareness that bondage is a lack; the cry can then rise. This explains the siman's statement that when Hashem wishes to rescue, He puts the cry into the person's heart. The later source context distinguishes freedom of understanding from continuing bodily exile.

records.themeTitle: The spoken words and the hidden heart
records.themeSummary: The closing verse includes what can be articulated and what remains hidden, with a demand to relinquish private motives.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains the same closing prayer verse through the Zohar's distinction between expressed words and inward matters that cannot be articulated. It then requires the person to remove private worldly interests. This gives a complementary account of asking that both mouth and heart be accepted, while preserving the siman's acknowledgment that the actual prayer may still contain distracting thoughts.
records.targetEnglish: It is written (Psalms 19:15), ‘May the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable before You…’ The Zohar says (Vayishlach 169a): King David said, ‘The words of my mouth’—these are expressed words; ‘the meditation of my heart’—these are hidden words that a person cannot express with his mouth, the meditation in the heart. One corresponds to the lower level and one to the upper level; expressed speech corresponds to the lower level. My holy grandfather explained that a person has actions in which he does not recognize Heaven's honor, to the point that he himself doubts whether his intention was clearly for Hashem's will. Actual mitzvot give him great assurance, for he knows that he fulfilled Hashem's will through them, as the Midrash says (Tanchuma, Ki Tavo): see what assurance and room to speak those who perform mitzvot have. But in ordinary optional matters he may doubt whether his intention was expressly to fulfill Hashem's will. This gives rise to accusations that perhaps this was not his intention. The counsel is to remove, from his side, every private interest, so that he has no worldly stake in these matters; then all the accusing powers will fall away.

records.themeTitle: Learning through seeing another's failure
records.themeSummary: The teaching reached after a failure need not require the learner's own failure.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef directly explains the siman's closing verse about seeing the recompense of the wicked. A person can learn from another's failure instead of undergoing or choosing it himself. This supports the siman's ordinary instruction to remain in Torah and refrain from anger, while the earlier discussion of exceptional purity remains qualified.
records.targetEnglish: Although many words of Torah can be attained only through toil, suffering and preceding failure—as Gittin 43a says, a person does not stand upon words of Torah unless he has stumbled in them—my holy grandfather explained that this too is only from the person's concealment. Because he distances himself from them, he needs toil, suffering and a preceding failure. In truth, even the teachings reached only through failure do not require that he himself fail. By seeing others who wish to distance themselves from Torah fail, one can likewise reach and understand those teachings. He need not fail personally; seeing another's failure suffices, as it says (Psalms 91:8), ‘You shall see the recompense of the wicked.’

records.themeTitle: Lasting Torah requires continuing attention
records.themeSummary: The recognition acquired through a mitzvah can remain, but cannot become a reason to abandon the work.
records.explanation: Tiferet Yosef explains the same difference between the time of a mitzvah's performance and the lasting effect of Torah. It then expressly warns against assuming that the acquired recognition makes further work unnecessary. This clarifies the siman's concluding claim that understanding and embodying a mitzvah's wisdom gives it an enduring presence.
records.targetEnglish: As the Talmud says (Sotah 21a), a mitzvah protects and rescues at the time one is occupied with it; Torah does so both while one is occupied with it and while one is not. A mitzvah means that at the time of doing it one sees Hashem's light. Torah means the holiness established permanently within oneself through the mitzvot; this established presence remains always. Although Torah too is described (Proverbs 23:5), ‘You cast your eyes upon it and it is gone,’ suggesting that Torah can sometimes cease from the person, this is when he turns his attention away and proceeds presumptuously: because he already had this recognition called Torah, he thinks that he needs no further work. Then it says, ‘You cast your eyes upon it and it is gone.’ But when he does not turn his attention away, it remains established in him both while he is occupied with it and while he is not.

records.themeTitle: Awe fixes remembrance in the heart
records.themeSummary: What is held with awe becomes a continuing presence rather than a passing thought.
records.explanation: Takanat HaShavin uses the same forgetting verse and calls forgetting the beginning of evil. It then supplies the positive mechanism: awe establishes the matter in the heart, where it remains present. This explains why the siman later requires awe for hearing and developing the continuing voice of Torah.
records.targetEnglish: Forgetting comes from the absence of awe, and it is the beginning of every evil, as it says, ‘If you forget… and follow other gods.’ Awe is the gate to the righteous person's courtyard. Through awe comes remembrance, for something a person regards with awe is fixed in the heart. Therefore Yoma 72b interprets ‘without a heart’ as the absence of awe. Something continually present in the heart cannot be forgotten.

records.targetRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Lech Lecha 31:7
records.themeTitle: The inward power of the sword and bow
records.themeSummary: The weapon image is read through prayer's inward force rather than physical reliance.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov raises the apparent contradiction between Yaakov's sword and bow and the psalm's denial of trust in weapons. It resolves this through their inward force, prayer and supplication. This clarifies the register in which the siman develops its more detailed distinction between nearby and distant spiritual work.
records.targetEnglish: His descendants followed him in recognizing that Hashem's life is found even in all this world's garments, and brought Heaven's honor into all worldly affairs. As the Zohar says (Vayishlach 173b), ‘Yaakov is the completion of the forebears; he grasps all sides, and called his name Israel…’ It is written of him (Genesis 48:22), ‘Which I took from the Emorite with my sword and bow.’ But, as the Sages explained, is it not written (Psalms 44:7), ‘I do not trust in my bow, and my sword will not save me’? He meant his power of prayer, as Bava Batra 123a explains, cited by Rashi, and as Onkelos translates, ‘With my prayer and supplication.’ He possessed the inward aspect of everything, including sword and bow, for the principal aspect of each thing is its inwardness (as explained in Vayechi, section 51).

records.themeTitle: Eightfold symbolism and the linen garments of inward entry
records.themeSummary: The symbolic eightfold account must be distinguished from the garments used for inward Yom Kippur service.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim expressly distinguishes golden garments from linen at the inward Yom Kippur entry and lists the four additional garments excluded there. The siman's reference to eight garments belongs to its symbolic account of eight modes of understanding; it must not be read as a literal description of wearing all eight in the Holy of Holies. This distinction is also relevant to the later garment discussion in Siman 263.
records.targetEnglish: This is also why the High Priest's service throughout the year was in golden garments: through his service he illuminated all the garments with the light of Hashem's will. But on Yom Kippur, when he enters the innermost place and Hashem reveals the light of His will explicitly without a garment, the High Priest does not stand before Hashem in such garments and expansion, but in linen garments, indicating that he then surrenders even the receiving vessel to Hashem. Thus the Sifrei says that bad, linen, is stated four times on Yom Kippur: one excludes the breastplate, one the ephod, one the robe, and one the forehead plate.

records.themeTitle: Entrusting the present level before receiving another
records.themeSummary: The soul-to-spirit progression is explained through surrender of the current attainment.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim cites the same progression from soul to spirit and explains that a person receives a further level by entrusting the present one to Hashem. This develops the relation between effort and gift in the siman without treating the numbered levels as achievements one can claim by intellect alone.
records.targetEnglish: In the order Hashem established in this world, in proportion to a person's surrender of himself to Hashem, Hashem returns to him a higher level. As the Zohar says (Mishpatim 94b), ‘When a person is born, he is given a soul from the side of the pure creature… If he merits more, he is given spirit.’ When this person can entrust his present level to Hashem, Hashem then trusts him with a higher level.
records.originHebrew: וְזָכָה יַתִּיר, יְהִיבִין לֵיהּ "רוּחַ" (זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב, צד עַמּוּד ב), הַיְינוּ כְּשֶׁנִּזְדַּכֵּךְ הַלֵּב יוֹתֵר עַד שֶׁהוּא מַרְגִּישׁ זֶה בַּלֵּב, וּבָא מִמַּדְרֵגַת אֱמוּנָה לְמַדְרֵגַת אֱמֶת, שֶׁהוּא הַדָּבָר הַבָּרוּר וְנִיכָּר לַלֵּב וְלֹא בֶּאֱמוּנָה לְבַד.
records.originEnglish: If he merits further, they grant him Ruach (Zohar II:94b), which occurs when the heart is refined until he feels this within his heart, advancing from the level of Faith (Emunah) to the level of Truth (Emet), which is clear and perceptible to the heart and not merely abstract belief.

records.themeTitle: Recognition becomes thanksgiving
records.themeSummary: Naftali recognizes the Giver in ordinary encounters and responds with thanks.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach gives a concrete form to the siman's movement from encountering the world to recognizing its Giver. Naftali immediately asks who made what he encounters, and recognition becomes thanksgiving. This supports the function of blessings described here without treating forgetting itself as a freely chosen act.
records.targetEnglish: ‘Naftali is a hind let loose, who gives beautiful words.’ He possessed a great understanding concerning everything in this world, immediately asking, ‘Who created these?’ This is the meaning of ‘who gives beautiful words’: since he recognized Hashem in everything, he gave thanks to Him. Thus Onkelos translates, ‘They will give thanks and bless for them.’
records.originHebrew: פֵּירוּשׁ, "אֱלֹהִים" – כֹּחַ וִיכֹלֶת בְּכָל מָקוֹם, וְהַיְינוּ בְּכָל שִׁימּוּשׁוֹ בְּכֹחוֹתָיו, בְּאֵיזֶה כֹּחַ מִכֹּחוֹת הַגּוּף: רְאִיָּה אוֹ שְׁמִיעָה אוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה אוֹ הִילוּךְ וְכַיּוֹצֵא, יַכִּיר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא הַנּוֹתֵן לוֹ כֹּחַ זֶה. וְזֶה טַעַם הַבְּרָכָה לִפְנֵי כָּל הֲנָאָה, וּבְלֹא בְּרָכָה – מָעַל (כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּרָכוֹת לה.); שֶׁהֲרֵי בֶּאֱמֶת קָדְשֵׁי שָׁמַיִם הוּא וְכֹחוֹת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְלֹא הוּתַּר אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי הַהַכָּרָה שֶׁהוּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְשֶׁהוּא הַנּוֹתֵן.
records.originEnglish: Meaning, elohim signifies power and ability everywhere, so that in all use of his faculties—in any bodily power: sight, hearing, physical action, walking, or the like—he must recognize that the Blessed Name is the One granting him this power. And this is the reason for a blessing before every physical pleasure, where without a blessing one commits sacrilege (Berakhot 35a); for in truth it is consecrated to Heaven and constitutes Hashem's powers, becoming permitted only through recognizing that it is from Hashem and that He is the Giver.

records.themeTitle: Degrees of attachment and future completion
records.themeSummary: Unbroken attachment is distinguished from the enduring purity of the inner root.
records.explanation: Resisei Layla treats the same statement about unavoidable iyun tefillah as incomplete attachment. It distinguishes the soul's root from surrounding faults while reserving fully equal, uninterrupted attachment for the future. This explains why the siman can speak honestly about an intrusive thought without identifying that thought with the person's essential root.
records.targetEnglish: Prayer means connection and attachment. This is iyun tefillah, from which no person escapes: even Yaakov is not completely perfected in having everyone equal and united without degrees of perfection and attachment. In the future, the Holy One will form a circle for the righteous, as stated at the end of Taanit 31a. A circle means that the level of circles will be revealed, where there are no degrees and everyone is equal in perfection. By contrast, Yaakov's stature is the upright form of a person, with degrees of head, end and extremities, as is known. One cannot escape—that is, attain complete perfection—for this power is not yet perfected until the coming of Mashiach, who will possess complete perfection. ‘As the leader, so the generation’ (Arakhin 17a): the entire generation will be completely perfected. They will then escape iyun tefillah as well, for there will be complete attachment, and consequently they will escape sinful thoughts and the dust of slander, which do not truly belong to the human person's own body.
records.originHebrew: כִּי מִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ נָקִי מִמַּחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת כָּל הַיּוֹם, לֹא יִמָּלֵט גַּם כֵּן מִמַּחֲשָׁבוֹת זָרוֹת בִּתְפִלָּה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא קסד.) דְּעִיּוּן תְּפִלָּה אֵין אָדָם נִיצּוֹל, וּמַשְׁמָע דְּעַל כָּל אָדָם קָאָמַר. וְאָתָאן דִּבְרֵי הַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי שֶׁהֵבִיאוּ הַתּוֹסָפוֹת (רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה טז:): "אֲנָא מִן יוֹמָא לָא כַּוְּונִית" כִּפְשָׁטֵיהּ, שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה אֶפְשָׁר לוֹ לְהִמָּלֵט בְּכָל הַתְּפִלָּה כֻּלָּהּ מִשּׁוּם נִצְנוּץ מַחֲשָׁבָה זָרָה.
records.originEnglish: for one who is not clean of alien thoughts throughout the day will not escape alien thoughts during prayer either, as written in Bava Batra 164b that from calculating expectation in prayer no man is saved, implying every person. And this brings us back to the Yerushalmi cited by Tosafot (Rosh Hashanah 16b): "In all my days I never achieved full concentration," according to its literal sense, that it was impossible to escape throughout the entire prayer from some spark of extraneous thought.
records.targetHebrew: ותפלה פירוש התחברות ודביקות, וזהו עיון תפלה דאין אדם ניצול, דבזה גם יעקב אין שלם לגמרי להיות כלו שוה וחד בלא מדרגות בענין השלימות והדביקות, וכמו לעתיד יעשה הקדוש ברוך הוא מחול לצדיקים וכולי (כמו שכתוב סוף תענית לא.), פירוש עיגול, דיתגלה מדרגת העיגולים דשם אין מדרגות דכלו שוה בשלימות. מה שאין כן קומת יעקב אבינו עליו השלום הוא קומת היושר דצורת אדם, שבזה יש מדרגות ראש וסוף וקצות כנודע, ואי אפשר להנצל דהיינו להגיע לשלימות גמור, כי כח זה עדין אינו בשלימות כנזכר עד ביאת משיח שהוא יהיה בתכלית השלימות. וכפרנס כן דור (כמו שכתוב ערכין יז.), כל הדור יהיה בתכלית השלימות ואז ינצלו גם מעיון תפלה דיהיה דביקות הגמור, וממילא ינצלו מהרהור עבירה ואבק לשון הרע, דהם אין שייכים באמת לגוף אדם.

records.themeTitle: The returning voice and effective speech
records.themeSummary: The rabbinic wind-and-rain example is explained through the relation between prayer and divine speech.
records.explanation: Dover Tzedek explains the same wind-and-rain examples through the returning voice: the voice of Torah and prayer rises and gives rise to a divine response whose speech is action. This clarifies the siman's use of praise as effective speech. These examples describe that relation; they do not say that every particular request must produce its requested visible result.
records.targetEnglish: A person's voice has an echo, as the Sages said (Shemot Rabbah 29). The voice of Torah and prayer rises above and pierces the heavens, as stated there in Shelach, and where it reaches it gives rise to a returning voice. The returning voice of prayer is as stated in Taanit and in HaPoalim: he said, ‘Who causes the wind to blow,’ and wind blew; ‘Who brings down rain,’ and rain came. This is the returning voice from his prayer. The heavenly voice proceeding from Hashem's mouth is likewise so. Hashem's speech counts as action, as stated at the beginning of the chapter Kol Kitvei (Shabbat 119b), and immediately wind blew and rain came through Hashem's heavenly voice. So too the statement (Berakhot 7a), ‘From where do we know that the Holy One prays?’ means that Israel's prayer gives rise to a returning voice above. As stated at the beginning of Berakhot, a heavenly voice coos like a dove three times daily: Israel's three daily prayers give rise to a heavenly voice from their own voice. It therefore coos like a dove, for the congregation of Israel is compared to a dove (Shabbat 49a).
records.originHebrew: וְאָז הֵם דְּבָרִים הַפּוֹעֲלִים, דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁהַשֶּׁבַח אֵינוֹ בְּדֶרֶךְ סִפּוּר דְּבָרִים לְבַד שֶׁזֶּה אֵינוֹ אֵצֶל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כִּי "בִּדְבַר ה' שָׁמַיִם נַעֲשׂוּ" (תְּהִלִּים לג, ו), וְדִבּוּרוֹ שֶׁל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ חָשׁוּב מַעֲשֶׂה. וּמֵאַחַר שֶׁשִּׁבְחוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם הוּא שְׁבָחָן שֶׁל צִבּוּר, הַיְינוּ דְּדִבּוּרָן שֶׁל צִבּוּר כְּאִלּוּ הוּא דִּבּוּרוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם, וְהַדִּבּוּר פּוֹעֵל יְשׁוּעוֹת.
records.originEnglish: And then these words effect reality, the praise not being mere storytelling—which does not exist with Hashem—for "by the word of Hashem were the heavens made" (Psalms 33:6), Hashem's speech being equivalent to action. And since the praise of the Omnipresent is the praise of the congregation, the speech of the congregation is like the speech of the Omnipresent, and speech effects salvations.
records.targetHebrew: כי הנה האדם יש לקולו בת קול כמו שאמרו חכמינו זכרונם לברכה (שמות רבה פרשה כ״ט), וקלא דאורייתא וצלותא סלקא לעילא ובקעא רקיעין כדאיתא בפרשת שלח שם, ובמקום שמגיע שם מוליד קול החוזר, והקלא דהדרא דתפלה הוא כענין שאמרו בתענית ובהפועלים: אמר "משיב הרוח" — נשיב זיקא, "מוריד הגשם" — אתא מיטרא, זהו הקלא דהדרא מתפלתו. והבת קול שיצא מפי השם יתברך גם כן כן, ודבורו של השם יתברך הוא כמעשה כמו שכתוב בפרק כל כתבי (שבת דף קי״ט ריש עמוד ב׳), ותכף נשיב זיקא ואתא מיטרא על ידי הבת קול דהשם יתברך, וכן מה שכתוב (ברכות דף ז׳ עמוד א׳): מנין שהקדוש ברוך הוא מתפלל? הינו בתפלתם של ישראל מולידים קול החוזר למעלה. וכמו שכתוב בריש ברכות: בת קול שמנהמת כיונה ושלשה פעמים ביום, והינו משלשה תפלות שבכל יום דישראל נולד בת קול מקולן של ישראל, ולכך מנהמת כיונה, דכנסת ישראל ליונה אמתילא (שבת דף מ״ט עמוד א׳).

records.themeTitle: The seventh and the inward point of freedom
records.themeSummary: Outward concealment does not erase the inner point described by seventh-year release.
records.explanation: Sod Yesharim reads ‘in the seventh she shall go free’ through the same inner point that cannot be enslaved. It distinguishes that point from the outward concealment in which servitude appears. This develops the siman's seventh-day and seventh-year correspondence; the source's Pesach setting is preserved rather than being presented as an identical account of every detail of Shabbat.
records.targetEnglish: As stated in the Zohar (Mishpatim 94): ‘If she is from the side of the Shekhinah, which is the seventh, certainly what is written? In the seventh she shall go free without payment.’ A soul from the side of a servant indicates concealment of the light, on account of which a little servitude is borne outwardly. But a soul from the side of the Shekhinah indicates the essential point of Israel, and that point does not bear any servitude at all. At the Exodus, that point's freedom was revealed without any concealment, for the light shone without an intervening screen. Concerning such illumination it says there, ‘But a soul from the side of the Shekhinah, which is the seventh—certainly what is written? In the seventh she shall go free without payment’: they went free from all four exiles.

records.themeTitle: The angel as the deed's spiritual power
records.themeSummary: The created angel is explained as the enduring spiritual power of the person's service.
records.explanation: Dover Tzedek explicitly defines the angel born from a mitzvah as the spiritual power of that human service. Its explanation of the angels' dependence on Israel's service clarifies the siman's account of an acquired power encouraging further good; it is more specific than simply repeating that one mitzvah leads to another.
records.targetEnglish: From all a person's service below, that service's spiritual power stands above as one of the heavenly host. This is the statement that an angel is created from every mitzvah. These are the heavenly watches, continuing ‘just as there are’—the Rosh's reading—and so forth. All the angels' service comes only through human service, as stated in the chapter Gid HaNasheh (Chullin 91b): ‘The angels do not say “Holy”…’ They then have permission and power [for they do not possess free choice; without permission they have no power] to say it—that is, reveal and publicize it—because Israel has already publicized it. Their power above is created and revealed as an angel, a spiritual power standing and serving on high, revealing the power of this service. This is the angels' service and song, which come only through Israel, and these are their three watches. See the beginning of the passage ‘If he holds.’

records.targetRef: Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Genesis, Vayeshev 1
records.themeTitle: Yaakov's dream as a source of Torah
records.themeSummary: The contrast with ordinary dreams includes Yaakov's study of the teaching within his dream.
records.explanation: Mei HaShiloach describes Yaakov examining his dream and teaching its depths to the tribes, who continued finding new Torah in it. This develops the siman's contrast between distracting dreams and Yaakov's dream. The surrounding passage reports the brothers' accusation concerning Yosef; that accusation is not presented here as an established judgment on his dreams.
records.targetEnglish: When Yaakov our father dreamed his dream on the way to Lavan, he began examining it and taught all the tribes the depth found in it. They studied it, and new teachings of Torah emerged for them each time, for many depths of Torah were found in this dream.

records.themeTitle: An involuntary occurrence does not prove a chosen thought
records.themeSummary: Takanat HaShavin expressly distinguishes an involuntary event from deliberately bringing it about through thought.
records.explanation: Takanat HaShavin discusses Adam's penitential years and insists that his involuntary occurrence did not follow a deliberate prior thought; otherwise the text would not call him a great pious person or describe it as involuntary. This is a necessary qualification when reading the siman's distinction between an occurrence built into bodily life and chosen wrongdoing. It does not erase the source's separate symbolic account of refinement.
records.targetEnglish: During those 130 years [Adam] spent fasting to return from his sin, he also produced spirits, demons and lilin through an involuntary seminal emission, as stated in Eruvin 18b. There he is called ‘a great pious person.’ Nevertheless, ‘even the most pious of the pious…’: his heart was not yet purified of bodily desire so as not to produce flesh, and through this he experienced impurity at night involuntarily. Although it was involuntary, he nevertheless produced spirits, demons and lilin and increased the power of the impure side, may the Merciful One protect us. Certainly it was not because he had entertained thoughts by day and violated ‘Guard yourself from every evil thing’—that one should not entertain thoughts, and so forth. Although the Torah had not yet been given to warn of this, they would not otherwise have called him ‘a great pious person.’ Nor would this have been called involuntary if he had brought it upon himself through his thoughts. Therefore he certainly guarded himself completely from every trace of such thought.

records.themeTitle: The Temple's face-to-face vision and remembrance
records.themeSummary: Temple vision is linked with remembrance and contrasted with the tower's forgetfulness.
records.explanation: Sichat Shedim uses the same verse about seeing the Master's face and explains the Temple as a place that strengthens remembrance. Its comparison with David's presence develops the siman's relation between recognition and revealed presence without making its three degrees of apprehension interchangeable.
records.targetEnglish: The place of the tower causes forgetting, as the Sages said (Sanhedrin 109a), the opposite of the Temple's air, which increased the power of remembrance. For ascent to the Temple is called in Scripture seeing ‘the face of the Master, Hashem’ (Exodus 23:17). Concerning seeing King David, the Sages said (Eruvin 64b) on ‘goodly to look upon’ (I Samuel 16:12): whoever saw him remembered his learning. All the more so the Master's face. The holy Zohar (II 163b) says: who is ‘the face of the Master, Hashem’? Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, for in truth it is the same matter. In particular this is King David, whose quality is known to be called by the name Adnut [the sefirah of kingship]. As I have also written elsewhere, the Temple's holiness in the dimension of world corresponds exactly to King David's holiness in the dimension of souls. Seeing him and his atmosphere likewise brought remembrance, the opposite of seeing the tower.

records.themeTitle: Achav's attempted claim was not vindicated
records.themeSummary: The parallel account explicitly records the failure of Achav's attempt to justify his killing through Gilad.
records.explanation: Dover Tzedek repeats this interpretation of Achav's proposed battle and adds its decisive outcome: he did not succeed. This keeps the siman's report of what Achav wanted to prove from being mistaken for approval of his claim that killing the prophets was righteous. The passage's own attribution of that attempted argument remains clear.
records.targetEnglish: [As I heard concerning the verse, ‘Do you know that Ramot Gilad belongs to us?’ (I Kings 22:3), and as it says, ‘Your hair is like a flock [of goats streaming] from Mount Gilad’: the hairs are judgments, indicating anger and killing, as is known, but from Mount Gilad it is the good form of killing, in accord with Hashem's will. Achav therefore sought to conquer Ramot Gilad, so that through this he would know that his killing of the prophets would be atoned for, as though it too had been killing in accord with Hashem's will. Therefore he did not succeed there.]

records.targetRef: Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 5:2
records.themeTitle: Recognizing providence in Mordechai's rescue
records.themeSummary: A second account of the same rescue emphasizes recognition within concealment.
records.explanation: Likkutei Maamarim asks the same question: why rescue Achashverosh when Esther needed deliverance? Here the answer emphasizes Mordechai's recognition that her situation belonged to divine providence even during concealment. This adds another aspect to the siman's analysis of correcting a personal motive; the two explanations are not presented as identical.
records.targetEnglish: This is the reason for Mordechai's intention in rescuing him from Bigtan and Teresh (Esther 2:21–23). Even during this intense darkness of slumber he understood ‘all that had happened’ (4:1), the purpose of it all, and knew the matter through the holy spirit. He apprehended that Esther's root was the root of the congregation of Israel, and that her being seized by Achashverosh was no accident. It would have seemed more fitting to rescue her and seek Achashverosh's death. He did not do so because he understood that everything was truly under Hashem's providence.

records.targetRef: Beit Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sara 4:6
records.themeTitle: Praying for the smallest possible deficiency
records.themeSummary: Recognizing ordinary human lack accompanies the effort to minimize it.
records.explanation: Beit Yaakov also discusses ‘a little folly,’ but first insists that a person pray for the inherited deficiency to be as fine as possible. Its later examples concern carefully guarded people whose unintended speech is clarified. This supports the siman's express ‘smallest possible’ qualification, rather than suggesting that one should deliberately create a fault.
records.targetEnglish: Mar Zutra said: ‘At a time of finding’ means finding a privy. In the West they said that Mar Zutra's interpretation is preferable to all the others: every pious person should pray for this. A privy indicates shame, meaning that a person should pray not to be put to shame. At the root, a deficiency is found in every person from birth. Hashem therefore created openings and cavities in a person, so that he should not become proud and imagine himself perfect in every respect. As the Talmud states (Bava Batra 75a), the Holy One said to Chiram king of Tyre, ‘I looked at you and created openings in the human person.’ This was said because he made himself a god. A person's openings indicate his lack of perfection: no person can be without deficiency, as it says (Ecclesiastes 7:20), ‘There is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin.’ This indicates deficiency at the root of each person's life. Therefore every person has surplus that is completely rejected and discharged: the excess of food and drink is not absorbed in his 248 limbs but is lost and rendered unfit. This indicates a deficiency present from birth; if there were only good in a person, from where would waste and surplus come? Every pious person should pray that this inherited deficiency be exceedingly fine and slight.

records.themeTitle: Torah as sustaining bread
records.themeSummary: The metaphor of nourishment includes Torah's sustaining life and the toil of acquiring it.
records.explanation: Kedushat Shabbat explicitly reads bread as Torah's sustenance and then connects the labor of bread with the toil of Torah. This explains the siman's description of Torah as actual nourishment for the soul. Its later account of purifying toil concerns devotion of one's vitality to learning, within the same nourishment metaphor.
records.targetEnglish: ‘All [a person's] toil is for his mouth’ (Ecclesiastes 6:7): its plain meaning concerns eating, for the mouth receives food to sustain his life. This is the purpose of all human service: sustaining his life and the life of the entire world. The whole world was created only for him and to accompany him, and he is equal to them all, as stated in Berakhot 6b, for they all depend on him. The Sages interpreted it in the chapter Chelek (Sanhedrin 99b) as toil in Torah. For ‘a person does not live by bread alone, but by everything proceeding from Hashem's mouth [does a person live]’ (Deuteronomy 8:3), which is within the bread, as is known. Concerning Torah it says, ‘Come, eat of My bread’ (Proverbs 9:5): it is the principal bread sustaining human life, as it says, ‘For it is your life’ (Deuteronomy 32:47). In Adam's curse it says, ‘By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread’ (Genesis 3:19), and toil in Torah was then decreed as well. As the Sages said (Berakhot 63b) on the verse, ‘Pressing milk brings forth butter, and pressing the nose [brings forth blood, and pressing anger brings forth strife]’ (Proverbs 30:33): this refers to the butter of Torah.

records.themeTitle: The annotator's reference conventions
records.themeSummary: A matching signed epilogue distinguishes editorial source references from the underlying manuscript.
records.explanation: This paragraph is the annotator Yisrael's notice, following the book's closing colophon. Here he distinguishes square-bracketed matter copied from the manuscript from round-parenthesized references he supplied. The Divrei Chalomot epilogue bears the same signature and explicitly uses round parentheses for his references in that work and Resisei Layla. It confirms that convention; it does not extend the square-bracket rule beyond what this notice actually says.
records.targetEnglish: The booklet Divrei Chalomot is completed, with Heaven's help. Yisrael said: I shall bless at the completion, for Hashem enabled me to mark the references in the book Resisei Layla and the booklet Divrei Chalomot. They are enclosed in two round halves, thus: (). May Hashem help us so that our master's words, may the memory of the righteous and holy be a blessing for life in the world to come, enter our hearts to love and revere Hashem, and so that our children and children's children engage in Torah and fear of Hashem all their days. Yisrael, son of my father, our teacher and master, the pious rabbi Yosef Yozel, of blessed memory for life in the world to come, of Lublin.
